newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil interest rates seen falling at same pace.
newsitem.headline: Brazil interest rates seen falling at same pace.

text.p: Brazilian policy-makers, confident the economy is not overheating, will probably cut the Central Bank's basic interest rate (TBC) to about 1.67 percent in February from 1.70 percent in January, economists said.
The Monetary Policy Committee will meet Wednesday to determine the new monthly rate, which serves as a reference rate for Central Bank rediscount lines.

"We think the government is going to stick to the same policy through the first quarter, so we expect to see cuts of about 3 or 4 basis points," said Elenora Santos, economist at Rio de Janeiro investment bank Fonte Cindam.

Despite a temptation to freeze interest rate cuts to curb demand and slow a burgeoning trade deficit, economists said the government would likely wait for more accurate information about the pace of economic activity before it decided to alter its current policy of gradual cuts.

Brazilian interest rate declines have slowed over the past six months after posting sharp declines in 1996. Real interest rates fell from 30 percent in 1995 to 15 percent in 1996. They are expected to fall to about 10 percent this year, economists said.

Another factor weighing on the Monetary Policy Committee's TBC decision will be the cupom, or the real return on fixed income investments based on exchange rate depreciation and nominal interest rates.
The cupom fell from about 17.5 percent at the end of 1995 to 13 percent today, which has slowed the inflow of speculative capital.

If the government sticks to its current exchange and interest rate policies, economists said the cupom would slip to an annual rate of about 10 percent in 1997. But they said policy-makers might shoot for an 11 percent cupom so as not to discourage investment flows.
